title: Domination-Avoiding Learning Agents Cannot Collude
claim: Some learning algorithms converge to the competitive equilibrium, while another settles on collusive prices well above it.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared axes, reference lines for Nash and monopoly
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the same axes. Each plots average price (y-axis, about 1.45 to 1.95) against training steps (x-axis, 0 to 1e6). The panels are titled Multiplicative Weights (MW), Follow the Perturbed Leader (FTPL) and Q-Learning. A shared legend above the panels shows a black solid line for the moving-average price (window 2000), a blue dashed line for the Nash price (1.47) and a red dashed line for the monopoly price (1.92). In the MW and FTPL panels, the black curve falls smoothly from about 1.68 and settles on the blue Nash line. In the Q-Learning panel the curve is noisy, with large jumps. It ends near 1.83, well above Nash and close to the monopoly line. The eye goes first to the contrast between the smooth curves and the jagged Q-Learning trace.
caption: Average pricing trajectories of learning agents in the Bertrand Logit duopoly game (typical run). Unlike Q-Learning (Right), which successfully coordinates on collusive prices, the no-regret algorithms MW (Left) and FTPL (Center) converge to the competitive Nash equilibrium.
abstract: An influential paper of Calvano et al. empirically demonstrated that Q-learning agents spontaneously collude when placed as sellers that compete on prices in a natural market model. More recent results of Fish et al. empirically demonstrated that similar collusion happens with commercial LLMs. We formally prove that such collusion can also happen with external-regret-minimizing agents. We identify a very general class of agents, which we term Domination-Avoiding agents, that provably do not collude in such markets. This class contains all Mean-Based agents and all internal-regret-minimizing agents, as well as others such as Multiplicative-Weight agents with variable learning rate and contextual variants thereof. More generally we show that, in any game, this class of agents is guaranteed to jointly learn to almost never play strategies that are eliminated by repeated elimination of purely dominated strategies.
